utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day starting with the Prosecution, please, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Bronagh McKenna, Dan Saxon, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone participating in the proceedings. Novak Lukic and Boris Zorko are representing Mr. Perisic today in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Again for the record, the Chamber is still sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis in Judge David's absence. And if we may just go through the ritual, Mr. Skrbic. Good morning to you. And can you just remember that are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. Thank you so much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try my best to stick to the time that I promised yesterday so, Mr. Skrbic, it will take a very short time before I hand you over to the Prosecution. During the proofing I went through you -- I went with you through Annex E of the indictment, and it relates to senior officers of the VRS. I asked you about particular individuals, and I'm going to divide this into two or three questions pertaining to specify areas. Now, first of all, I'm going to ask about yourself. In the indictment, the Prosecution in Annex E to the indictment, under the subtitle of "Department for Mobilisation and Personnel," the Prosecutor claims that starting from June 1994, Major-General Petar Skrbic took over the duty from Grubor, and then it says as follows: "In December of 1995, Skrbic was nominally promoted to the rank of major in the Army of Yugoslavia." Now, Mr. Skrbic, do you agree with what the Prosecutor claims here, that is to say that in 1995, in December of that year, you were formally or nominally promoted to a rank in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, is it formally or nominally? The English translation said formally or nominally. Those -- I mean, those are two different things.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading the original in B/C/S and the word is "nominal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to make certain corrections in the title that I had. I was not chief of the department. I was, rather, head of the sector, and I think that also in English there is a distinction between the two. So I was the head of the sector for organisation and mobilisation affairs. Your Honours, I wanted to ask you whether we are talking about nominal appointment or formal appointment. I was formally appointed or promoted in 1995 to the rank of major-general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you're asking the Bench, paragraph (F) under this heading, Department for Mobilisation and Personnel Affairs, they said beginning in June 1994, Major-General Petar Skrbic assumed Grubor's duties. In December 1995 Skrbic was nominally promoted to the rank of major-general in the VJ. That's what I read in the English Annex E to the indictment. Now, nominally means something different from formally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can anyone explain to me what "nominally" means? Is that actually?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am reluctant to try and explain what the Prosecutor meant by the word "nominally." I should leave it up to the Prosecution in cross-examination. However, as for all other individuals mentioned in Annex E, the Prosecutor always says that they were nominally promoted or the only one who was nominally appointed to the VJ was Mr. Skrbic, and they are using the same term, "nominally." Probably the Prosecutor is going to explain this in their final brief. As I understand the word "nominally," something very close to "formally," although you think there is a distinction. So let me rephrase the question that I want to ask Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, essentially and actually, where were you promoted to the rank of major-general, in the VRS or in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And was that promotion any different from the promotion of any other of your colleagues in the -- in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was no difference. All of us were actually and essentially promoted in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And -- okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to move now to another set of facts alleged by the Prosecutor to be pertaining to a number of individuals. For example, in Schedule E, the Prosecutor claims about Momir Talic, Lieutenant-General Bosko Kelecevic, Boric Grujo, Novica Simic, and Zivomere Ninkovic, the same thing by using the same phrase, i.e., that is to say that in October 1993, the VJ postponed the final decision on the promotion pending a report from General Mladic. You remember we went through this yesterday. All these individuals that I named are linked to October and November of 1993, which is the time when you were not yet in the Main Staff of the VRS or for that matter not in the VRS at all. My question is: From the moment when you were appointed to the duty of the assistant commander of the sector that has a long name, are you aware whether for any verification of the ranks of general Mr. Mladic's opinion had been sought?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I collected this from several passages, but I will give you a reference for you, Your Honours, to be able to follow. I was quoting the facts where it says, the 1st Krajina Corps, and then under (a) and (b), then the 2nd Krajina Corps under (a), the Eastern Bosnia Corps under (a), and air force and antiaircraft defence under 8. The Prosecutor alleges the same thing for all these individuals mentioned therein. In October of 1993, the VJ decided to postpone the decision on their promotion pending a report from General Mladic, so each of these individuals has this sentence attached to their name. I just put them together in one and the same group because of the same context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You can get your answer from the witness. The witness has not answered you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Skrbic, you understood my question. From the moment when you took over your duty and you explained to us how involved you were in the verification of the ranks of general in your sector, are you aware that for any of those verification an opinion of Mr. Mladic or General Mladic was sought?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list of the generals who were promoted in the Army of Republika Srpska was submitted to the 30th Personnel Centre. It went without saying that this list should have looked at by General Mladic and that he gave his opinion. As we saw in one of the exhibits, he put the word "no" next to one of the name. So this kind of list was then also submitted to the 30th Personnel Centre for the sake of preparation of certain documents for verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us try to be more precise. After submitting this list, do you know whether anyone from the VJ asked the opinion of Mr. Mladic regarding the verification? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether from the General Staff of the VJ through the 30th Personnel Centre asked your sector to provide additional information about any of the general for whom the verification of the rank was sought?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked them for their opinion nor were they authorised to offer any opinions about this group of generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Three individuals mentioned in the indictment --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if Your Honours would just bear with me for a moment because I would like to go through this quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says in the indictment that the person under (B) Budimir Gavric, under the heading "Eastern Bosnia Corps," and the person under (b) from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, Dragomir Milosevic, that their promotion was rejected because of their links with the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's just not sufficient to say the person under (b). You've got to tell us what part of the indictment are you reading. Are you still on Annex E?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, but it wasn't probably recorded. I'm still on Schedule E, the section relating to Eastern Bosnian Corps under (b) General Budimir Gavric, and also from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from the next page under (b) General Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What about them?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's the same sentence attached to the both names, namely that their promotion to the VJ had been rejected because they had links with the SDS. You can see that, that the identical sentence was used for both individuals. Can we please move to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will have two more questions concerning Schedule E. Under the Drina Corps and (a) in relation to Major-General Milankovic, the Prosecution invokes a document and states that when he was relieved of his duty, General Zivanovic, interpreter's correction, it is stated that he was posted to a new position within the VJ/VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can counsel please slow down with quoting because the interpreters didn't find the actual reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter requested that you slow down when you're quoting because they don't have the reference. They don't have the document before them to read, so they can't interpret what you're saying. So can you try to be very slow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will read as it is stated here. In the Drina Corps heading, under the Drina Corps heading under (a), General Zivanovic, the Prosecution makes reference to a document where it is state that: "When Zivanovic was relieved of his duty as commander, that Major-General Radoslav Krstic, father's name Milorad, assumed the post of corps commander, and Major-General Milenko Zivanovic the previous co-commander was appointed to new duties in the VJ-VRS." Now, my question is: When General Zivanovic was relieved of his duty as commander, do you know what became of him afterwards?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milenko Zivanovic was retired. He wasn't assigned anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a question relating to another individual, but let us be careful because of interpretation. I'm interested in the heading under "Air force and anti-aircraft defence," under (b), Bozo Novak. The indictment alleges as follows: "In September 1996, it was decided by the VJ that Novak be recalled and placed at the disposal of the VJ. He was later retired at the end of 1996." Do you know that General Bozo Novak was recalled from his duty in the VRS by the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It -- I almost myself objected to what Mr. Lukic asked me because I don't understand his question. I know everything there is to know about General Novak, but what it is that Mr. Lukic wants me to say. I can, even if not asked a question, tell you the story concerning him, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, whenever you are asked a question you do not understand, it is your right to say, "I don't understand your question." So don't hesitate to object on that basis if you call that an objection. Just tell him, "I don't understand your question. Could you rephrase." Because you must answer a question that you understand so that you tell us what you know. Rephrase your question, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to do that because I merely read out what the indictment said, and I'll repeat my question. If you can't answer, tell me so. Do you know, General Skrbic, that the Army of Yugoslavia recalled General Bozo Novak from his duty in the Army of Republika Srpska? I think that now it should be quite understandable.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that. It wasn't the Army of Yugoslavia that recalled him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I've completed this part, and I just have two questions left, General, and then I'll be done. And I do apologise if it was your understanding that I took up too much of your time.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was just joking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard during your testimony that you used to see Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Mladic, and Mr. Perisic, that you were in their company. Can you tell us on the basis of these encounters what was their relationship between President Milosevic and General Perisic -- General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it between Milosevic and Perisic or Milosevic and Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have two questions. My first question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You must ask one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the way I had put it to the witness. Yes, I do apologise to the interpreters. Again I'm sorry, I apologise to the interpreters if I misspoke. I don't know mind whether we do this in public session or private session. It is really up to you, witness. President Milosevic and General Mladic, I would like to ask you about their relationship.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, up to the moment when that name was mentioned, and you know which one it was, I can give answers in open session. The relationship between President Milosevic, the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and for a while the President of Serbia as well, who was in both capacities a member of the Supreme Defence Council of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the one hand and General Mladic on the other hand, may I explain this very briefly. It was a relationship of courtesy. They respected their respective roles. Mladic thought that the president was saying political things and that did he not have a good attitude towards the Army of Yugoslavia, and he said that to him quite openly at one point in time. Sometimes he behaved to him in a feisty way, but it was my opinion that President Milosevic did respect him. That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you explain the relationship between General Mladic and General Perisic on the basis of the facts that you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That relationship between General Mladic and General Perisic was a very complex one, in my opinion. I shall explain it now just in terms of certain categories that there's no need for me to explain really. Namely, that means that it was a comradely relationship, that there was a certain degree of respect involved. Also, that there was ignorance involved sometimes -- or, rather, ignoring and sometimes even underestimation, especially from General Mladic towards General Perisic. But General Perisic would sometimes respond in kind. It was my impression that sometimes the communication was even banal. Sometimes they even addressed each other as if they were on close terms, but I don't think that that was their true relationship. All in all, their relationship was truly highly complex. I do apologise to Mr. Perisic if I'm saying something here that are perhaps not exactly pleasant for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally hear, or did you hear from others that Perisic ever issued any kind of order to Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Your Honours, I have completed my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [Previous translation continues] ... very long 15 minutes. Mr. Saxon. Mr. Saxon, yesterday I think you -- I don't know whether you were here or it was just Mr. Harmon, the witness wanted to know how much longer he's going to be kept. Are you able to guesstimate your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not think that I will finish today. I think it's most likely now it will be Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Did you hear that, Mr. Skrbic? This is to your question yesterday about how long you're likely to be here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It all fits in, Your Honour. There's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, General Skrbic. My name is Dan Saxon, and I'm representing the Prosecution today. I've got some questions for you. Before I start, as Judge Moloto instructed you previously, please if you do not understand my questions, simply stop me and ask me to rephrase that, and I'll be happy to do so. It won't be the first time. I'm sure it will not be the last time. Secondly, I'd ask -- I will try to ask my questions as clearly as I can, and I'd ask that you try to listen to my question as best as you can and provide me with hopefully relatively brief answers when you can. Do we understand each other?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too, Mr. Saxon. I have fully understood what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. General, I'm aware, obviously, of your successful military career. You started out you were trained in anti-aircraft rocketry. By the time you retired, you were a lieutenant-general. And I'm also aware of your impressive academic background. I understand you have a degree in military psychology and sociology. You've got a Masters Degree in political science, and I note that you have published articles on topics ranging from the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia and as well on questions of morale in military units. And, in fact, even today earlier in the transcript, I think it was at page 11, lines 7 to 11, when you were describing your time as a member of the Main Staff of the VRS, you explained how it was important for high-ranking military officers to contemplate political issues both domestic and international. And I'd like to focus, if we can, please, first on how you used your academic expertise and your knowledge to assist you in your work first as a JNA officer and later as a VJ officer working in the Administration for Morale and Information Affairs and then later on in the 2nd Krajina Corps of the VRS. And maybe we should just start with some of the basics, General. Just fundamentally, in a military sense, it's important for armies to monitor the morale of their officers and soldiers because during wartime if morale is poor, chances are the soldiers won't fight very well. Do you agree with that? Am I right on that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I agree. They will not be fighting properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Now, on Monday, the first day of your testimony, and this is at page 11558 of the transcript, you testified briefly how in July 1991 you joined a group within the Ministry of Defence of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, a group which analysed the way in which the JNA was viewed and analysed by the mass media across Yugoslavia. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. However, I don't know what it's called in English, but in Serbian, I did not actually become a member of, et cetera. I was actually ordered to join this group that was involved in that particular work. Sorry, I was no member of anything whatsoever. I was an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me. I stand corrected, General. And you also testified that in its report this group concluded that a survey of the media concluded that the JNA was under increasing attacks by the media and it produced a study which was prepared for the Federal Executive Council. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that. That's what I said, and you have just said that properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, on page 11558, lines 11 through 18, you mentioned how in general terms this group reviewed mass media, and you mentioned mass media from Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro, and Macedonia. So can you describe this process? Help us understand it a little bit more, please. When you say your group reviewed the mass media, are you -- would you be including, for example, the daily newspapers?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, we analysed everything, daily newspapers, press clippings that were submitted to us by a certain institution. Some officers monitored the radio and others monitored television but only with regard to the topics that are involved here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. And how about weekly magazines, magazines like "Vreme," for example, weekly news magazines?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I don't seem to recall that at the time "Vreme" was being published at all. However, in Serbia we did follow "Nin" in particular. As for the magazine "Vreme" I cannot remember exactly, so I do apologise, but I cannot give you a specific answer. If it was being published at the time, then we were certainly following that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And I can -- I imagine, sir, that you contributed your expertise in performing comprehensive research and analysis to guide other personnel in that group who were reviewing this material; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, that group was headed by Colonel Mile Susnjar, and I was his deputy. The two of us provided instructions as to how the media was to be followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe those instructions for us?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you a brief description. We would give certain persons an assignment to follow, say, "Politika," "Vecernje Novosti," "Mladina" from Slovenia and other newspapers, and we tell them not to read everything, not to waste time but just to read up on the articles where the JNA is mentioned and how the JNA is mentioned in these articles, and then they prepare that for the daily report that we compiled, and then we carried out a monthly analysis. "Mladina" from Slovenia was practically in its entirety devoted to attacks against the JNA. They had to read that in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I imagine other persons were given the assignment to do something similar with television broadcasts and radio broadcasts; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it was much easier to follow TV, because that information about the JNA, regardless of whether it was positive or negative, was brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, General, after the JNA became the VJ in 1992 and the Administration for Morale and Information became part of the General Staff of the VJ, I know that you became eventually deputy chief of the -- of the Administration for Morale and Information. And no doubt during 1992 and 1993, critical years, at least until December 1993, you ensured that the Administration for Morale and Information continued to monitor the mass media in the former Yugoslavia for information that could affect the morale of VJ personnel. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is right basically, but I was no longer in that group for following how the media treated the army. I was transferred to the administration that you gave the name of, properly so, and then I started dealing with the question of morale in the Army of Yugoslavia. I'm not sure, but I think that this group actually ceased to exist, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lest there be any misunderstanding, I think that Mr. Saxon should be very specific in his question, especially when in line 21 he says that the mass media in the former Yugoslavia should be followed, 1992 and 1993. Which mass media did he expect this administration to follow? Did Mr. Saxon mean media outside the FRY at the time and, if so, could his question be very specific in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to get to that, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe, General, at the time you became the deputy chief of the Administration for Morale and Information, what instructions did you give to your subordinates vis-a-vis monitoring the media?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I received my orders from the chief of administration who was my superior. He was the one who issued instructions as to what kind of work the department should do with regard to the effects on the morale. I did that only in technical terms, without changing anything in the essence of these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, can you describe the instructions that were issued by the chief of the administration regarding following the media for issues that might affect the morale of VJ soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a particular instruction on building, monitoring, and improving the morale of the army. Pursuant to that instruction, we received information from subordinate units, but only relating to the factors that have either positive or negative effects on the morale. Also, other details were elaborately presented in that instruction. I am doing my best to give you the shortest possible answer, but this is a complex matter, if you agree with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, let me see if I can ask my question a different way. While you were the assistant -- the assistant chief or the deputy chief at the Administration for Morale and Information in the Army of Yugoslavia, were there personnel who as part of their duties in that administration monitored the media?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not within that department. There was a smaller department compared to the group that he had spoken of before, but as they're co-workers, we used some of their information. I couldn't order them to provide any such information, but could I tell the chief of administration that we needed this particular information, and we would eventually get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. And are you able to tell us in public session the name of this department that was doing this media monitoring?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can say that. It was called the Department for Information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us, this Department for Information, then, no doubt monitored information that came out in the media, did it not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this Department for Information, no doubt, periodically would have synthesised or collected important information that came out in the media and produced periodic reports for other members of the General Staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Saxon. Not only periodically but after the war started in the neighbourhood, they provided daily information about what the media wrote about. I think it was called a bulletin, and it was published on a daily basis. If you have any information where this particular publication is called differently, I'm sorry, but I think it was called a bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you so much, sir. And no doubt you would have received these daily bulletins; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And no doubt sometimes these daily bulletins contained information that had been circulated in the media that might affect the morale of VJ personnel; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes, and particular pieces of information, but not all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sure. Very well. And these bulletins would also go to the other members of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, including the Chief of the General Staff, or at least the office of the Chief of the General Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only to the Chief of the General Staff, who at the time was General Zivota Panic, but also to all members of the General Staff who had the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. And the same system, though, was in place -- maybe I should step back for a moment, General. I know that you left for Republika Srpska in December of 1993, but before that, in the months previous to that, say from August 1993 until December 1993, this same system of the circulation of an information -- circulation of a bulletin from the information department, that same system existed; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was working in the administration this system was operating continually, but after that I took up the position of the director of military publishing house, and I didn't carry out these duties any longer. I don't know what happened with the systems in the aftermath. After my departure, this administration was totally revamped, and I personally disagreed with that, but that's how it was done. And I don't know how the system continued to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And tell us, please, when you took up the position of the director of the military publishing house, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date. I hope the Chamber won't mind that. I took over the duty, but I never carried it out for a minute because I left and joined the VRS. I think that it coincided with the period sometime in mid-1993, but I don't recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. These daily bulletins, if you will, they contained information taken from media reports from throughout the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until 1992, it was from the whole of the former Yugoslavia. After at that it was reduced to Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Montenegro, Macedonia, and Serbia. There were no comments in those bulletins of any kind. No one was allowed to provide their judgmental opinions. They were just required to report what the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina and elsewhere were writing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sure. And those bulletins would also have included particular information that was reported prominently in the international media; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Information that was reported are -- actually, I'll stop here for a moment. Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. I need to show the witness an exhibit and work through it with him and that will take some time. Could we perhaps take the first break now and come back at a quarter to 11.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break and come back at a quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, before the break we were talking about the production and circulation of the bulletin, the daily bulletin from the information department, and on page 28 of today's LiveNote transcript, starting at line 10, you noted that while you were working in the administration of the General Staff of the VJ for morale and information, the daily bulletin system was operating continually, but after you took up your position as the director of the military publishing house, you don't know what happened with the system -- with this system in the aftermath, and my question for you is: Do you have any reason to believe that after you took up your duties as the director of the military publishing house approximately in mid 1993, that the chief of the General Staff or the chiefs of the administrations and the General Staff stopped receiving this media information?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I object, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that any answer provided by the witness would be pure speculation. He said in his previous answer that he didn't know what happened afterwards, so I think that whatever is going to be elicited from this witness is going to be pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not asking the witness to speculate. I'm asking him a factual question. I'm asking him whether he personally has any reason to believe that this daily bulletin system stopped in mid 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question will be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you want me to repeat my question, General Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need for that, Mr. Saxon, but again I can only surmise what happened. In view of the fact that this administration had been reorganised, I suppose that it continued to operate for a certain period of time and that after that it stopped operating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you are surmising. You have no factual knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Also before the break, General Skrbic, you mentioned that -- this is at page 29. You acknowledged that these daily bulletins would also have included particular information that was reported prominently in the international media. So if you can recall, for example -- if we just focus right now, for example, on international television, would this bulletin have included reports from television stations such as BBC, Sky News, CNN?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. We monitored the broadcast of these media outlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And with respect to international radio, would the bulletin also have included information coming from, for example, the Voice of America?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only radio station that we followed. We didn't listen to any other radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With respect to the print media or news agencies, would the bulletin have included information from news agencies such as Reuters or the Associated Press?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, one reason why it was important for the Department of Information to monitor information coming out of the mass media at that time was because some of that information concerned issues of security pertaining to the VJ and the former Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may only add the JNA, the Army of Yugoslavia, and the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And activities of international organisations such as NATO and United Nations in parts of the former Yugoslavia were also important to security, wasn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show General Skrbic what is Exhibit P2870, please. And could we please zoom in a bit on the B/C/S version when this comes up and a bit in the English version as well. Yes. If we can zoom in. You will see on the right-hand side, if we can zoom in on that article where you see some yellow highlight. Thank you so much. Maybe even zoom in just a little bit more if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, I'll give you a moment to take a look at the first few paragraphs of this article. It's an article that was originally published in the Belgrade daily "Politika," on the 14th of August, 1993. It appears to be sort of political commentary by a man named Miroslav Lazanski, and it's entitled "Recall Vietnam." And you'll see in the first paragraph the author is talking about possibilities that NATO might bomb certain targets in Bosnia. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if it would be fair to the witness to see what the date of this article is. All I can see is that in the English version it says the 14th of August, 1993. I think that would be useful for the witness to be able to find his bearing in the article.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Saxon mentioned the 14th of August, 1993, and I, myself, can see that that is correct. Mr. Saxon, I have read this first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, although the print is not very large, would it assist you to read off of a hard copy? Would it just make your life a bit easier right now? It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm fine with the screen, and I said that I have read only the first paragraph. Do I need to read the whole article?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, sir. I want to ask you right now something about what's said just in that first paragraph. And actually, it may be at the start of the second paragraph, Your Honour, General Skrbic. It says that: "We are witnesses of television screens in which Manfred Werner, General-Secretary of NATO, is absolutely grinning with joy that bomber squadrons at the Aviano base are ready for action." Do you see that sentence there? I believe in your version it's the beginning of the first paragraph -- it's the second paragraph, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, and I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question goes back now to these daily bulletins and the information service. Would it have been the responsibility of those officers who received -- who found such an article like this from "Politika" to have gone back, then, to the -- perhaps the original media reports that are referred to here such as these television scenes of the General-Secretary of NATO? Would that have been part of the responsibility?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understood your question, but I can tell you this: The analyst's duty was to include this military political commentary into the body of information, and after that they would make comparisons. So they would focus on the particular subject, whether it be NATO or whatever. If we had time, we would analyse it and compare the sources, but as I said, at the time I was not part of that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So when you say, "If we had time we would analyse and compare the sources," you mean the sources that are referred to, for example, in an article like this one, television, "Washington Post," "New York Times?"

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before I showed you this particular document, General Skrbic, you acknowledged that information about the activities of NATO, United -- or the United Nations in the former Yugoslavia were important because they might -- they might affect the security of the FRY, of the VJ. Can you recall what kind of events or activities of NATO or of UNPROFOR were reflected in these bulletins? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only recall the situation where NATO imposed a no-fly zone above Bosnia-Herzegovina and that they monitored the situation by radar on AWACS. And as for the rest, I can't remember what we analysed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you recall whether these bulletins would have contained information about the deployment and operations of units of UNPROFOR in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We would come across such information too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And obviously, then, these bulletins also would have included information about the activities of the Army of Republika Srpska, the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. The department that was charged with monitoring the information, and I wasn't in that department, would follow the press coverage. They wouldn't go beyond that. For instance, if Mr. Lazanski wrote an article on these events, then of course the department would analyse those topics too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General, it was my mistake, I think. My question was not clear. That's what I meant. In other words, these daily bulletins would have included information from the media about the activities, military activities, political activities, going on in Republika Srpska, Republic of Serbian Krajina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. General Skrbic, I'd like to move to a different topic now. Actually, not so different perhaps. Let's -- let's fast forward a bit to when you became a member of the Army of Republika Srpska. I know that you were first in charge of morale and information and legal affairs in the 2nd Krajina Corps, and then in mid-1994 you moved to the VRS Main Staff. Can you tell us what kind of system or procedure was in place in the VRS to provide high-ranking officers like yourself with important information coming from the media?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't a worked-out system, Mr. Saxon. We had to deal with that ourselves. We did not have such groups within the VRS that would analyse the media. We were left to our own devices in that regard. You're asking me about the time when I assumed my duties in -- in that army. Of course, in the Main Staff there was something of that sort, but we were simply short of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe what -- what did exist in the Main Staff in this regard?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the VRS Main Staff there existed a centre which was detached from the department for morale, religious and legal affairs. It was an independent analytical group charged with monitoring the issues we're discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. And this independent analytical group, how often would it produce -- I don't know what you might -- what you call them at the VRS Main Staff: Bulletins, reports? How often did that occur?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't produce anything, Mr. Saxon. Rather, they would orally convey information to the commander of the Main Staff, as well as to the general who was tasked with the field of morale, religious and legal affairs. It may have so happened that they would write a report here and there, but they were not duty-bound to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And depending on the information and the importance of the information and, to use a term that you have used, "the need to know," would some of this information then have been passed on orally to other members of the Main Staff as well?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information would have been passed only in cases, which were very rare, where the specific topic would concern one of the high-ranking officers or commanders. There was a strict selection in place. In times of war you can't simply swamp people with great amounts of information. You can do that in peacetime. In wartime you don't have time enough to engage in thorough analyses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Understood, General, understood, but that is sort of the point that I'm interested in. Because of the demands of wartime, important information that was reported in the media would have been brought to the attention, at least to the chief of the VRS Main Staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. You said earlier that -- I'll try to find what you said just a few moments ago. "We had to deal with that ourselves. In other words, we had to deal with access to media information ourselves." This is at page 36. You said: "We did not have such groups within the VRS that would analyse the media. We were left to our own devices in that regard." Did you individually find ways to get access to media information, to keep up on the, you know, national, international, political and military issues that might affect the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, let me underline one important difference or to draw a distinction, and that's the fact that in the 2nd Krajina Corps I had to take it upon myself to get hold of information, and that's what I did. I read papers wherever I could. I watched TV whenever I was able to. And that's the major difference compared to the Main Staff. When I was transferred to the Main Staff, I didn't ask for such information, I didn't look for such information, and I didn't need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page 38, 2, the witness said that they listened to the radio -- he listened to the radio when he could and that he didn't have a TV, and this isn't reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Lukic, the transcript says: "I watched TV whenever I was able to." Now, you say you said he never had -- he didn't have a TV and he listened to radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what he said, but you can ask the witness directly. I don't want to interpret him. He can repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Mr. Saxon, can you ask the witness the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, my -- my original question was: "Did you individually find ways to get access to media information, to keep up on the national, international, political, and military issues that might affect the VRS?" And then you began to respond, talking about an important difference, and perhaps if you could repeat your response for -- for the Chamber and the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can repeat what I said. While I was occupying the duty in the 2nd Krajina Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska, I was forced to draw on -- on my own resources and to follow the media that I was technically able to. When I was transferred to the Main Staff of the VRS, this wasn't an area of interest to me. I could hear information as a private citizen, but I did not follow it officially. Was I clear enough now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, you were, but I'd like to ask a follow-up question, sir. With respect to your comment about when you were part of the 2nd Krajina Corps and you were following the media that you were technically able to do, can you be a bit more specific? During that period of time, what kind of media were you technically able to follow?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could continually follow the radio. We had TV sets, but the image could not be transmitted because of interference which existed throughout that time in the area of Drvar. We also did not receive newspapers on a regular basis. I think it was only the "Srpski Glas" paper that we received regularly. For the rest it depended on the war conditions. In the 2nd Krajina Corps we received the bulletin "Vojska Army" of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And did you also continue to receive the bulletin "Vojska" of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You said during this period when you were in the 2nd Krajina Corps you had TV sets but the image could not be transmitted. Was the sound available?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The interference was complete, and I didn't know where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Saxon. At times you would get the image and then it would be lost again. So it was very difficult to cover. Then we had power outages as well, so you couldn't follow the radio either. That was the actual state of affairs, but I'm trying to shorten my answers and I'm not explaining all these things. I apologise to everyone if at times my sentence turns out to be appear contradictory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No. Your sentences are fine. It's very clear. Thank you, General. I want to move to another topic now. I want to bring -- bring you back, General, to some testimony that you gave earlier this week. I can't recall right now whether it was Monday or Tuesday, but it's at pages 11600 to 11601 of the transcript, and Mr. Lukic was asking you some questions about persons who left the FRY to join the Army of Republika Srpska, and in response to one of Mr. Lukic's questions, you said that you were not aware that VJ officers were coerced by threats of early retirement unless they agreed to join the ranks of the VRS. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you remind me again what my answer was? Did I deny this fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I wouldn't quite say that. You said that you were -- I'll start again. Mr. Lukic asked you whether you were aware whether VJ officers were coerced by, for example, threats of punishment such as early retirement, unless they agreed to join the ranks of the VRS. And your response was, no, you were not aware of this. Is that clear now?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's clear, Mr. Saxon. I'm quite clear on that now. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you a document, if I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit P2827, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, I'd like to give you a moment to familiarise yourself with this document. You'll see it's from the 3rd Army command of the VJ. It's dated the 26th of September, 1994, and it's addressed to the commands of the Nis and Pristina Corps and the 201st Anti-armour Battalion Command, and the first paragraph says: "Following the orders given by the chief of the VJ Main Staff at the meeting held on 5 September 1994, and the records kept within the personnel administration of the VJ Main Staff, regarding those officers who failed to follow the order on deployment as well as the officers who left the units of the 40th Personnel Centre of their own will --"

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, I'm not receiving interpretation at all times because I seem to be -- the voice seems to be fading at times. I don't know if it's a technical problem. Should the interpreter come closer to the microphone or something just to increase the volume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. We don't know what it is caused by. Can ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe with the volume increased let's see whether you can hear now. Could we do a test, please. Could the interpreter say something to the witness, "Testing, testing, testing," something like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear it now a bit better, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Sorry for that interruption, Mr. Saxon. Could you rephrase your question or restate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, let's start again. Have you had a chance to review the first paragraph of the document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have, but you haven't read it fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. Not yet. And it says at the end: "... it is necessary to do the following: "1. Establish the whereabouts of officers deployed to the 40th Personnel Centre units from your basic units. "2. Urgently inform the personnel of the 3rd Army command by telegram in case any of these persons return to the 40th Personnel Centre main composition. "3. Pass on the order by the chief of the VJ Main Staff to all persons who left the 40th Personnel Centre units of their own will, or failed to carry out the deployment order into the 40th Personnel Centre, that they are required to report to the meeting with the chief of the VJ Main Staff," and then it gives --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have a problem, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not me personally, but the question relates to the 40th Personnel Centre. In order to save everyone's time, can I please ask you not to put questions to me concerning the 40th Personnel Centre since I'm not competent in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you're not competent when the question is put, just say, "I don't know anything about that." If you don't know anything, you don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Skrbic. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll take that as a compliment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Take it as a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then there's an instruction to report to the meeting at the address and the date and time. And then you'll see, and if we can scroll down in both versions, please, you will see there's a list of names there, General. Can we go to the next page in the English version, please. And if you could, I just want to draw your attention, General, for now to two names on this list, number 3, Mraovic Zeljko, warrant officer 1st Class serving in the Nis Corps; and number 9, Djuro Sakic, warrant officer 1st Class, serving in the 201st Anti-Armour Battalion. And could we please go to the next page in B/C/S, please. General, you'll see at the top of page 2 in the version in Serbo-Croat that Lieutenant-General Samardzic is saying: "A written report is to be delivered before either 30 or 29 September 1994, at 10.00, for the purpose of preparing a report for the chief of the VJ Main Staff regarding the officers who are required to attend the meeting with the chief of the VJ Main Staff." Are you able to read that there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we leave this document, please, and can we show the witness Exhibit P1865.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, this document is dated the 7th of October, 1994. It's from the 3rd Army command, and in the preamble underneath the word "Urgent," it says: "Pursuant to the order of the VJ General Staff chief," and there's a number, "and after interviews of the professional officers and non-commissioned officers with the VJ General Staff chief regarding transfer and appointment to the 40th Personnel Centre, I order." And then you'll see under heading 1 there's a group of officers who are to be put into operation order on transfer and appointment to the 40th Personnel Centre. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know why I'm looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just be patient with me, General, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we scroll down in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in the -- at the start of the bottom half of the page we see -- we see the phrase "Rim 2." Do you know what that abbreviation stands for, General Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roman 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you know what the Roman numeral 2 is like? I don't need to remind you. It's a double I in the Latin alphabet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. It says "Roman numeral 2, to initiate procedure for termination of professional military service for the following." And then we see the names of the two officers that I had asked you to pay attention to in the last document, Mraovic, Zeljko, the warrant officer, and Sakic, Djuro, another warrant officer, and it says: "On the meeting held with the chief of the VJ General Staff, the above-mentioned persons have stated that they would like to terminate their professional military service with their right for retirement." Are you able to follow me?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please go to -- the last paragraph talks about scheduling an official interview regarding their request for termination of professional military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please go to the next page in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, General, you'll see at the top of page 2 the first paragraph says: "In case that the above-named do not want to terminate their professional military service upon their request, they are to be referred to report to units of the 40th Personnel Centre in the period regulated by point 1 of this order." My question for you, General, is that doesn't this indicate that effectively Warrant Officer Mraovic and Warrant Officer Sakic were given two choices: Report to the 40th Personnel Centre, or end their professional military service. Isn't that what these two documents indicate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's an embellishment of the statement, Mr. Saxon. This document doesn't say report or terminate. It says report to 40th and they choose to terminate. It's at their request. Let's not mislead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They choose to -- they choose to terminate when they are being called upon to go to the 40th Personnel Centre it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see Judge Picard is shaking her head, Your Honour, so I'm not quite sure which Your Honour I need to be responding to, and perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you understand what Judge Picard said by the shaking of her head, would you please respond to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you'll give me a moment, please. Your Honour, we -- I can perhaps rephrase my question a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you should.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- let me try to rephrase my question, and I'm going to try to -- well, never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One reasonable interpretation of this document, General Skrbic, is that if these two officers were not going to terminate their military service, they would have to report to the 40th Personnel Centre; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Skrbic is here to testify about facts that he knows about, not to assess documents. Now he's being asked to provide his opinion about a certain document that Mr. Saxon is putting to him, and in this way he is supposed to go into the sphere of speculation. My question was very fair. I mean, the proposition I made, the answer that he gave during the examination-in-chief was fair, and if Mr. Saxon wants to challenge that, he has to put it that way to the witness. I think that this question simply calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any time, Mr. Saxon. You are entitled to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I'm a bit surprised by Mr. Lukic's objection in that he asked this witness on direct examination about his opinions on numerous, numerous documents about what was happening, what relationships were being affected by different documents, and clearly this witness was a lieutenant-general, extremely -- he's extremely qualified to give his opinion on what can be interpreted in a military document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: First of all, is your back okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's all right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see you're holding it, and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's all right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I find myself in a difficult situation, because, yes, Mr. Lukic may have asked those questions of the witness, but those were questions in relation to areas that the witness had worked in. The witness, with respect to this document, has actually requested not to be asked questions about the 40th Personnel Centre, and the Chamber said to him if he doesn't know the answer to the question he must just say he doesn't know, because it's not for the Chamber to restrict counsel on what questions to ask. Now, if he is being asked to express an opinion about things that happened in the 40th Personnel Centre about which he says he has no knowledge, I think that puts that question in a slightly different category from the category of questions that were asked where he was being asked about his field of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then I will move on, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, I want to talk to you about the period when you went from the VJ to serve in the Army of Republika Srpska in December 1993. Just so that I understand, I want to clarify something, part of your testimony under direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And my question relates to testimony of General Skrbic and page 11604 of the transcript, lines 21 through 25. If I may have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, at this part of your direct examination in response to a question from Mr. Lukic, you told the Trial Chamber: "I must tell Their Honours that for three months I was the general manager of the military publishing centre with the Army of Yugoslavia. However, after the three months, I became a full member of the Army of the Republika Srpska as part of the 2nd Krajina Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska when I signed a document on the hand-over of duties." Do you recall that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon. However, I don't know why it is reflected that way in the transcript, because there is a bit of imprecision there, a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is there something you'd like to correct, sir, or make more precise?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, may I just tell you that as for being director of a military publishing centre, I never received that duty. For three months I was director or general manager in formal terms, but I was transferred to the Army of Republika Srpska. After those three months, I became a member of the Army of Republika Srpska, and I signed a document on the hand-over of duty in the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So if I can just make the chronology clear. Since you were transferred to the Army of Republika Srpska in December 1993, then you would have been the director or general manager of the military publishing centre from September 1993 until December 1993. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From the 17th from December, and then three months on. That's when I was director, in formal terms. As for that duty, that is the director of the publishing centre, I never carried out those duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Just so the record is clear, I just want to ask a follow-up question or two. You're transferred to the Army of Republika Srpska on the 17th of December, 1993, and for your first three months of service in the 2nd Krajina Corps of the VRS, at least in a formal sense you also held the position of the director of the military publishing centre of the Army of Yugoslavia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise for the delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, I want to talk about your transfer to the VRS in December of 1993. In the Army of Yugoslavia, there was a procedure created by the Law on the Army for termination of professional military service. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And although I know you were transferred in December of 1993, if you'll permit me to refer to articles -- I believe it's Articles 111 through 114 of the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, that law -- those are the articles at that deal with termination of professional military service from the version of the law that was created in 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that these articles are not correct, because I recall that it was Article 107 and another one, but I do remember for sure that Article 107 says something about the termination of professional military service. However, please don't take my word for it. I don't have the law in front of me. Perhaps Mr. Saxon is actually putting it accurately, because I don't know which version of the law he has.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Actually, I'm grateful to you, General Skrbic. I was putting it partially accurately, and I'm glad you made me more accurate. You're absolutely correct. I mistakenly did not include Article 107, and I should have, which is entitled "Reasons for Termination of Professional Military Service." You're absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, can we talk about some other little point. You say those articles were created in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm referring to these articles as they are stated in the Law of the VJ of 1994, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After he went to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct. And I have a follow-up question to try to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you went to the VRS in December 1993, were there in the older Law on the Army, I guess it was the law --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic is kindly trying to correct something that I said. I -- all right. I'll keep going.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I assume that in the Law of the Armed Forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that was still in place when you were transferred to the VRS, there were similar articles, similar procedures for termination of military service; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, that is correct what you said. They were similar but not identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. When you were transferred to serve in the VRS, your service in the VJ was not terminated, was it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: De facto, yes. Formally, it went on for another three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Formally, you say, it went on for another three months. So does that mean three months later you received an official VJ document terminating your service?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not receive such a document. The document on the basis of which my service in the VJ was terminated is called the report on the hand-over of duty. And I do apologise for drawing your attention to that report yet again. That was the document that meant that I had taken over this duty in the Army of Republika Srpska and that I had become a member of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But it certainly was not a document terminating your status as a member of the Army of Yugoslavia, was it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. My status in the VJ was not terminated, but I was serving in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Now, when your professional military service in the Army of Yugoslavia ended pursuant to a decree of the president of the FRY on 31 December 2000, you received a document at that time terminating your military service in the Army of Yugoslavia, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that this date is correct though. I think that I retired on the 1st of April, 2001, on the basis of a degree issued by the president of Yugoslavia, Mr. Vojislav Kostunica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But the decree of the president was dated the 31st of December, 2000, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Saxon, but that is the decree on the termination of service. However, yet another document is passed and that is the decision on the termination of service, because during those three months, from the 1st of January until the 1st of April, I was still available, and my service as such was terminated by this document called the order on hand-over, and I can explain why that is what it is called. You return all your equipment, your uniforms, et cetera, then once that has been done then you say good-bye and they say good-bye to you and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we take the second break at this time, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, we may, if you have no use for the remaining minutes. We will come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. General Skrbic's microphones need to be turned on, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I just have a few questions for you, General Skrbic, regarding your transfer to the VRS in December of 1993. You were transferred, in fact, pursuant to an order of the chief of the personnel administration of the VJ General Staff, dated the 21st of December, 1993. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. At that time -- maybe I should say that month, December 1993, can you recall how many other VJ officers received such orders?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you recall perhaps specific individuals, specific individual VJ officers, colleagues of yours, perhaps, who were transferred to the VRS at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but it will take some effort on my part to tell you the name. One of them was Colonel Despotovic, and the other man's name was Nebojsa, who was an officer and a film director by occupation. These are the only two names that I can remember at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall what position in the VRS Colonel Despotovic filled?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, do I. I remember, Mr. Saxon, because General Milovanovic had asked him, "What is your profession, Colonel?" And he says that he was a physiotherapist, and then he said, "You will remain in the VRS in order to provide treatment for me." Maybe that person can help you too. I'm sorry for this joke.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No. I was going to say what a shame Colonel Despotovic isn't here right now. And the officer who was a film director by occupation, can you recall what position in the VRS that person filled?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember him being appointed to the sector for morale, religious affairs with General Gvero, but I don't remember exactly which position he filled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This order, for example, transferring you to the 30th Personnel Centre, was that a written order or a verbal order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it was a written order, but I wasn't much interested in that because I had decided to join the VRS and that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You never received a copy of this -- of a written order transferring you to the VRS, did you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
