utterances.text: Yes, did I receive it, but I don't remember its content.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where would we find such an order? Where we would find a copy of this order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question, Mr. Saxon. I can only make a supposition, but I don't think that would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. General Skrbic, can you recall what undertakings were given in those orders? What was the content of the order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought he just said he doesn't remember the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did he say that, Your Honour, or did he say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line 11, page 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I stand corrected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Tell me, General Skrbic, the VJ officers who received these orders transferring them to the 30th Personnel Centre, such as the one you received in December 1993, did the VJ officers have to obey the orders?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this order, they had an attitude of taking it voluntarily. They were supposed to obey it, but it was up to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand that response, General. Now, it's my understanding that in any modern army an order is an order. Orders are given so that they are obeyed. Now, is my general understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will give you an explanation taking my personal example. I know what an order is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I need to stop you there for a moment, please, sir. I want you to answer my question. Is my general understanding correct as I just expressed it to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your understanding is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to hear your additional explanation, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to explain my personal example. I knew what an order meant, but I was entitled to say no, I'm not joining the VRS, and after that, and I knew that for sure, I would not have faced any consequences or any sanctions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, you've just accepted that generally speaking, orders were orders. They had to be obeyed. If orders had to be obeyed, why would you not face any consequences if you had disobeyed this specific order? Is there any reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because there was no legal basis for taking any sanctions against such individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, if I can ask a follow-up question to that last response to His Honour Judge Moloto. You say there was no legal basis for taking any sanctions against such individuals. Is that because there was no basis in the law of the -- law on the armed forces of the SFRY or the law on the Army of Yugoslavia -- let me -- let me stop there and try to ask a clearer question. You say that there was no legal basis for taking any sanctions against such individuals. Is that because under the law of Yugoslavia, as it existed at that time, there was no legal basis for the VJ to be sending its officers to fight outside the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, you had a more competent witness here than I am, who could have provided a better explanation than I can. What I can say is that I personally volunteered to join the VRS, but I didn't want to go without any document. If you want an official vehicle to be driven, you have to have a paper that goes with it. So I didn't want to go over there without any documents. It is possible that experts found some legal basis for issuing such kind of documents, but I cannot explain that to you. All I know and all I was interested in was that I joined the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was there a legal basis for the Army of Yugoslavia to transfer its officers to a foreign army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There must have been some kind of provision in that respect, but I cannot remember. It's not formulated for an army, but probably it says a different department or -- or the positions filled by military attaches or labour organisations that were involved in special-purpose production. All that was provided for in the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That I understand. That's just being transferred within the same army of -- of Yugoslavia. But to the best of your memory, was there a legal -- legal provision within the law on the Army of Yugoslavia that allowed the Army of Yugoslavia, for instance, to say to you, "Now go and join the Russian army. Get out of here. Get out of the VJ and go join the Russian army?" Was there such a legal basis, to the best of your memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as I know there wasn't such provision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, I want to follow up on a comment that you made shortly before Judge Moloto's last question. You say, "What I can --" this is what you said, page 57, starting at line 12: "What I can say is that I personally volunteered to join the VRS, but I didn't want to go without any document." And then you say: "If you want an official vehicle to be driven, you have to have a paper that goes with it. So I didn't want to go over there without any documents." And the reason you didn't want to go to the Army of Republika Srpska without any documents is because you needed to have official permission or clearance from the Army of Yugoslavia because otherwise you would have been going AWOL. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you as a career military officer, a very competent, obviously, military officer, didn't want to do anything that would jeopardise your career, your reputation, with the Army of Yugoslavia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, all I was concerned about is not to jeopardise my family, because I was going to war, Mr. Saxon. I could have been killed. Therefore, I wanted to have at least a document on the basis of which my family could have claimed certain rights, because then and now my family is living in Belgrade. I wasn't much interested in my career. You remember me saying that I was prepared to go and fight in trenches like an ordinary soldier. I was not interested in my career, and I'm not offended by your questions. I just want you to know what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's fine, and I appreciate that response, General. The bottom line is, though, you needed to maintain your membership in the Army of Yugoslavia so that your family would maintain their rights and be taken care of while you were serving in the Army of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so, Mr. Saxon, and thank you for providing such a precise definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I may come back to this topic, but I'm going to move on for the time being. General Skrbic -- General Skrbic, during your direct examination with Mr. Lukic, at pages 11736 to 11737 of the transcript, Mr. Lukic asked you the following, he said: "Do you know if during the war, at the time when you took up your position in the Main Staff, some of the members of the VRS went to attend command staff schools, specialised schools, or the School of National Defence of the Army of Yugoslavia?" And your response was the following: "The position of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska was that those who had graduated from the military academy need not attend post-graduate schools because the war itself was the best of schooling. So during the war we did not send a single individual to attend any of these schools." Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And as far as I could discern, you have quoted my reply accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness Exhibit P867, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, you'll see that this is an order from the Drina Corps command, signed by Major-General Zivanovic, on the 18th of July, 1994. It's entitled "Training for 30 combatants in Pancevo Special Battalion." And it says that the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade will refer 30 combatants from the Manoeuvre Battalion, to the Special Battalion Pancevo Garrison in the period between 25 July and 10 August 1994." And in number 2 it says that: "The Yugoslav Army Special Unit Corps will regulate the intake, accommodation, nourishment, and training of combatants." Have you been able to following along with me, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But in the middle of the page above the phrase that says "I hereby order," it also says -- it says it's pursuant to an order of the General Staff of the VRS, dated 15 July, 1994, and "... our demand for performing special training for some of our units." This document demonstrates that certain members of the Army of the Republika Srpska received training by the Army of Yugoslavia during the armed conflict. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon, but this has nothing to do with what I was talking about, higher military education. This is training, whereas schooling and training in the VRS were very much different. In addition to that, I would like to draw your attention that here we're talking about combatants who had attended no school whatsoever before that, let alone be sent to attend some higher schools. And my remarks are well meant and well intended in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I understand that, General. Now, one way to maintain and improve the morale of soldiers is to provide them with good training. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how much this is deriving from my examination-in-chief. Mr. Saxon read my question and the answer relating to higher education in military service, whereas he has moved to training. I asked no questions about training, and the witness decidedly said that his sector had nothing to do with training, and that is what he said in his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, Your Honour. However, Rule 90(h)(ii) does not restrict me to topics covered by counsel during direct examination, and this is a topic that is relevant to the case of the Prosecution, and I want to explore it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My only concern with the way you put your question is that you link it to -- you link it with higher education, military education when you say, "But the bottom line is." You're suggesting that notwithstanding you, Mr. Witness, saying that you talked about higher education and not training, I'm still saying to you that the bottom line is that these people received training from the VJ. He's never testified about whether people did or did not receive training from the VJ. He testified about whether people went for higher education in the military academy, and I think if you just want to ask about whether people did go for military training with the VJ you can ask that, but when you link the two, I think again we're sort of tampering with the evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Point is taken, Your Honour, and my apologies to the Chamber and to General Skrbic if I -- if the structure end of my cross was misleading in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can say, let's deal with a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let us deal, General Skrbic, with the topic of training if we can do that, all right? And my question for you is: One way of maintaining and improving the morale of soldiers is to provide them with good training. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please leave this exhibit and show the witness what is Exhibit P931, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, you will see this document is a report from the tactical live fire exercise with the rocket Strela 2-M in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And if we can just stop there for a moment. I know that you have a background in anti-aircraft rockets. Is the Strela 2-M a sophisticated weapon for anti-aircraft defence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, very sophisticated but very simple in terms of anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. This report, you will see, talks about 46 soldiers from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps who first received some initial training in Banja Luka and then proceeded for live fire training with senior officers in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia where they were accommodated at the Batajnica barracks in Belgrade. That's in the middle of the page. Do you see that? Can we scroll down in the English -- in the B/C/S. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What am I supposed to read, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No. I just asked if you have read that portion, that's all. I just want to make sure you're seeing what the document says, that's all.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've hardly read anything, so could you please indicate to me which paragraph I'm supposed to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. There is a paragraph beginning -- I believe it's the third full paragraph from the bottom in your version, beginning with "Upon the completion." Do you see that paragraph? You will see that paragraph describes 42 VRS soldiers who were accommodated in the VJ barracks at Batajnica where in December 1994 they trained with the Strela rocket launcher and training simulators. The next paragraph -- are you following with me, General Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. The next paragraph talks about the fact that there was classroom training. There was a theoretical part of this training. A daily plane flyover was organised so that the officers involved could train with real targets that were arriving and departing, which led to live fire training on the 9th of December, 1994. And then in the very -- one the very last sentences, the author of this document, Lieutenant-Colonel Trncic, says, "This was a real example of how training for Strela operators should be conducted." This kind of training was provided to members of the VRS, so in this case these members of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, so that they could carry out their operations more proficiently; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I waited for Mr. Saxon to finish in order to provide a general objection to this line of questioning. I noticed that Mr. Saxon, a few moments ago, referred to 90(h) and the right to ask every witness that appears in this courtroom -- ask about facts that have to do with his testimony. However, there is no doubt that this was not brought up at all during the direct examination. What we see here is something that appeared in the Prosecution case, what we see on the screen now, and the Prosecution concluded that this document was sufficient per se for their case. Now, in my view, Mr. Saxon is re-opening his case through the back door, if I can put it that way. This document had nothing to do whatsoever with the testimony of this witness or the direct examination. In this way he is trying to get to new facts that are important for his case. I think that this line of questioning, now that the Prosecution case is over, is actually a re-opening of the Prosecution case and that is why I oppose this line of questioning in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, I'm not aware of any authority, certainly from this Tribunal, that supports the position of Mr. Lukic. Second of all, I am not re-opening my case. I am asking this witness to comment on evidence that -- yes, that has been admitted in this trial. There is nothing from the Prlic jurisprudence, for example, or I believe nothing from the Delic jurisprudence that classifies evidence that has been already admitted -- or questions stemming from evidence that has already been admitted as fresh evidence. This witness is here. This witness has a particular expertise and understanding and knowledge, and I'm trying to explore a facet of his knowledge. Now, that -- that -- if I'm not allowed to do that, then quite frankly I think a large part of Rule 90(h)(ii) is then gutted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very brief. The Prosecutor had the document during his case. He had expert witnesses who testified. I'm not going to refer to their names, because they were protected witnesses. He did not put any questions in this regard. I think that that is why the Prosecution is dealing with this document now, a document of his own that he didn't want to use at all during his own case. Now he is trying to re-open his case through this document during the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're done?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you done? "That's not correct," that's what you want -- that's your response? I want to come in now --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- again, yes, the Prosecution is not restricted in cross-examining the witness. Cross-examination can go in various directions. What, however, causes me concern, and I hope the Bench, is the fact that Mr. Skrbic has not denied that training was provided by the VJ to the VRS, quite apart from having not testified about that. He's now being asked to comment on this document when he doesn't have prior knowledge of it. Yes, he has knowledge of anti-aircraft rockets. He was trained in rockets, but I'm not quite sure where the Prosecution is going with this kind of cross-examination of this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- because I think the Prosecution has made its case that there was that kind of training which this witness is not denying. Beyond not denying it, I'm not sure what it is you want from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a few points that you made there, and I'm going to try to respond to them, if I may. First of all, if the witness is not able to answer the question of the Prosecution related to this document, that's fine, and of course that may be -- that may be a very normal turn of events. But the position of the Prosecution is the Prosecution should not be precluded from asking its questions, okay? First of all -- I mean, if Mr. Lukic is correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're commenting on my points? I never said you absolutely should be precluded from asking questions. I actually said the opposite. I said you can go at large. But I'm saying what I do not -- I'm trying to follow the cross-examination, and I'm trying to say, and I know the bulk of my understanding will come during final arguments, but as the case goes on, I'm trying to follow what counsel is trying to establish with the witness. Now, to the extent that this witness has not denied any training of combatants of the VRS by the VJ, I'm not quite certain where counsel is going with the further questions beyond that point. That's all I've said. I haven't said you're precluded from doing anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For example, Your Honour, I asked a question a short time ago that, for example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question that made Mr. Lukic rise on his feet, yeah. That's have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This -- page 64, this -- line 18. "This kind of training was provided to members of the VRS, so in this case these members of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, so that they could carry out their operations more proficiently; is that right?" That was my question, Your Honour. And depending on the answer that I was going to get, I was going to ask a follow-up question as well based on -- I have of in front of me, I have a career military officer who also served in both the VJ and the VRS, who has obviously experience and knowledge of the events that were occurring during the time of the indictment period, some of which involved training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then the objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, would you like me to repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This kind of training, the Strela rocket training, was provided to members of the VRS - in this case they were members of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps - so that they could carry out their operations more proficiently; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer to this question. If you want to hear me as an expert, and I am not one, at this point in time I do not have that status, you can remove these documents and ask me about anti-aircraft defence, especially about training for Strela 1 and Strela 2. Then I'm going to give you answers. I don't need any documents for that. I did not dealing with training in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, I'm sorry, I can't accept that response. You were a career military officer. You personally had training, for example, in anti-aircraft rockets. Let me start from a more general question. The purpose of training soldiers and officers is to help them become more proficient in their duties. Isn't that right? In general terms.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. No one can deny that for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So in the particular case of this document, we've got soldiers who are being trained to make them more proficient in the use of these rockets; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trained in Republika Srpska, and they had more possibilities for gaining greater knowledge there because they actually did have sorties with weapons, Mr. Saxon. I have to see which period this refers to. Well, I cannot see it, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, this document refers to the training of a group of soldiers from Sarajevo-Romanija Corps who travelled to Batajnica near Belgrade to receive this training. Do you -- do you understood that? That's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Now, will you agree that this training would have made these particular military personnel more proficient in the use of this anti-aircraft system?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single military officer from any army in the world could dispute that for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there's no dispute, is there, that becoming more proficient is going to assist one's morale in any military. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This kind of simplified conclusion cannot be drawn, unfortunately. It has to be proven. In order to become more morally capable, you have to know something that will affect you, Mr. Saxon. The question is how much the actual soldiers knew about this. I see this document for the very first time in my life. So now if you're going to ask me how training affects morale, it's actually the other way around: How does morale affect training? Where is education inserted into the process? We can discuss that, and I'm prepared to do that. However, if you are going to use general questions to lead me through a specific document, I'm afraid you're going to get logical answers rather than specific ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you'll give me one moment, please. Line 63 I asked you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said line or page?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Page 63, line 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I asked you: "One way of improving the morale of soldiers is to provide them with good training. Isn't that right?" Your response was: "Quite right." So are you stepping back from your earlier testimony?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not stepping back, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note that there is still some time left in this session. However, I probably have at least another session worth of questions, so I'm not going to finish today. As, you know, my back is not a hundred per cent. Would it be possible to adjourn at this moment until Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought before the break you said your back was fine when I asked you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I mean -- I did say that, Your Honour, and I'm prepared to carry on if you want me to carry on. I didn't want to stand there and complain about my back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't want to make you carry on if you're not feeling well. You say you're not well right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. If you want me to carry on I will, Your Honour. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. It's not in the nature of this Chamber to force people to do work when they are not in a position to do it, particularly when the reason is related to health. Okay. We will take a break. Unfortunately, then, Mr. Skrbic -- there we have it now -- who is that therapist -- physiotherapist now? He's not here, it would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Despotovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Despotovic, okay. Once again, Mr. Skrbic, you are not supposed to talk to anybody about the case until you are excused from testifying, I'll just remind you of that. We will come back to court on Monday, the 21st of June at 9.00 in the morning in the same courtroom. We will take an adjournment until 9.00 Monday morning. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of June, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.24 p.m.,
